A tag under a protest post still does something a rec- ommendation engine cannot: it lets a stranger on the other side of the world find the exact same conversation on pur- pose, not because a system decided they might like it. That distinction matters more than it first appears. An algorithm optimises for engagement, not for solidarity. It will happily show one person a protest and another an unrelated distraction, each convinced they are seeing what every- one else sees. A hashtag, however crude, offered something closer to a shared ad- dress, a place where strangers could ar- rive by choice rather than by inference.
What we lose when machines do the sorting Perhaps the more interesting question isn't whether hashtags survive, but what their decline reveals about how we now relate to information itself. For most of internet history, finding something re- quired a small act of intention. You typed a word, chose a tag, joined a thread. Increasingly, relevance is handed to us before we ask for it. That shift is not neutral. It changes the posture we bring to discovery, from active searching to passive receiving. There is something worth noticing in that change, not necessarily something to fear. Every generation inherits new tools for making sense of an unmanage- able amount of information and every generation eventually watches those tools get quietly replaced by something more efficient and less visible. A strong hook line, a repeated phrase, a shift in pace before the final image: these devices exist be- cause the human brain is still, at its core, an oral processor. Psychologists study- ing working memory have found that we retain rhythmic, patterned information far more easily than flat prose. A poem read silently on a page asks the eye to do the work. A poem spoken aloud asks the whole nervous system to listen. Why the algorithm feels like an old town square There is something almost uncanny about watching a spoken word reel go viral. The format, sixty to ninety sec- onds, direct address to the camera, a build toward one sharp closing line, mir- rors the structure of oral storytelling per- formed for a live crowd centuries ago. The troubadours of medieval Europe travelled between courts reciting verse for immediate reaction. Griots per- formed for a gathered village, adjusting tone and emphasis based on the room's mood. Today's poets perform for an au- dience they cannot see, but the feedback, in the form of comments, shares and duets, arrives just as fast, sometimes faster. or in the moment of its utterance. Walter Benjamin wrote about the aura of an original work, the sense that something performed live carries a weight a mere copy cannot replicate. A voice note com- plicates that idea beautifully. It is both a copy, saved and replayed endlessly and an original, carrying the particular breath, hesitation and emotion of one person at one moment. Listeners often say a voice note from a loved one feels more alive than the same words typed out. That feeling is not sentimental exag- geration. It reflects something real about how humans process tone, pitch and pace as carriers of meaning that text alone cannot hold.
What is gained and what quietly disappears Not everything about this shift is un- complicated. Written poetry rewards slowness, the kind of attention that lets a reader return to a line and sit with it. Spoken and recorded poetry often moves at the pace of a feed, designed to be con- sumed once and scrolled past. Some poets worry that nuance gets sacrificed for immediacy, that the quiet, difficult poem loses out to the one built for a pun- chy ending. Yet something valuable is also being recovered. For generations who grew up without confident access to written lit- erary spaces, whether due to language, education or simple distance from pub- lishing centres, the spoken and recorded form removes a barrier that print quietly built up over centuries. A poem no longer needs to pass through an editor's desk to reach a reader. It only needs a voice and a willingness to press record. Grandparents who could never engage with a printed poem in English now listen to their grandchildren's verses translated through the warmth of a famil- iar voice.
A memory older than the page Perhaps that is the quiet truth sitting beneath this whole shift. Poetry was never really a written art form that occa- sionally got performed. It was always a spoken art form that, for a few centuries, got written down for convenience. The voice note and the reel are not poetry's future breaking from its past. They are poetry remembering where it came from, using tools its earliest makers could never have imagined but would likely recognise instantly: rhythm, breath, an audience and the simple, ancient act of one voice reaching another. ■
